posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
The day’s activity closed at eighty-eight feeder visits, more than double the recent average of forty-seven for this time. This steady flow contrasts with the quieter mornings of the previous week, where only twenty-two visits were recorded on Wednesday. The Tufted Titmouse remains the station's primary visitor, accounting for forty-nine confirmed feeds across the twelve hours of light.

The auditory record highlights a persistent chorus of Eastern Towhees and American Crows, with the latter reaching a peak of thirty detections in the 16:00 hour. A Blue Jay contributed significantly to the evening soundscape, logging sixteen detections in the 18:00 hour before the light failed. These vocalizations filled the gaps between the visual visits that characterized the midday period.

As dusk approached, the feeder traffic thinned but the air remained active with sound. The final visual record belongs to a Tufted Titmouse, seen six hundred and sixty minutes after sunrise, just before sunset. The day ended with eleven species documented, a count that exceeds the recent average of nine by a notable margin.

posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
Feeder traffic has continued to outpace recent days, with seventy-five visits logged so far against an average of forty. Tufted Titmice remain the dominant presence, their last confirmed sighting at 16:06, twenty-three hours into the light period. Carolina Chickadees and Mourning Doves have made steady visits through the morning and early afternoon.

The soundscape is dominated by Eastern Towhees and American Crows, with the Towhees particularly active during the 10:00 and 11:00 hours. A Blue Jay was heard in the 15:00 hour. The weather is mild, with a high of 25.8 C and light winds.

A male Northern Cardinal was seen approaching a seed bowl from the grassy area. The station has recorded eleven species so far.

posts.heading: September 12, 2026
posts.text:
The morning began with a Carolina Wren’s call in the 06:00 hour, thirty-one detections so far. At 07:50, a Tufted Titmouse became the first bird seen on the feeder, thirty-eight minutes after sunrise, and has since accounted for twenty-seven visits. As of 10:30, traffic is higher than recent averages, with fifty-five visits and eleven species recorded against a typical thirty-two visits.

By 08:00, the soundscape shifted to twenty-two American Crow detections and fourteen Eastern Towhees. A male Northern Cardinal approached a seed bowl from the grassy area at 08:51. The feeder remained active through 10:30, with the last visual logged at 196 minutes after sunrise by a Blue Jay.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The afternoon quiet ended with a distinct evening surge, as Carolina Wrens logged nine additional detections and American Crows added three in the 19:00 hour. This final burst brought the day's total to one hundred and three feeder visits, significantly exceeding the recent average of thirty-three.

The last visual record of the day belongs to an American Crow, seen seven hundred and nine minutes after sunrise near the water bowl. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees maintained their dominance at the feeders, while the American Goldfinch remains the station’s first confident visual record of the species.

The sound and sight counts reflect a busier day than the recent norm, with the Wren’s persistent chorus bridging the gap from early morning calls to the final dusk detections.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text: The Carolina Wren continues to dominate the soundscape, with six additional detections logged in the 15:00 hour to sustain the day’s high vocal count. A single Red-bellied Woodpecker was heard at 14:00. The weather holds steady with a high of 30.1 C and light winds. The last visual record of the day so far belongs to a Ruby-throated Hummingbird, observed three hundred and forty-five minutes after sunrise. Twelve species detected compared to the recent average of seven.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The Carolina Wren was already calling before the first light hit the yard, with forty-eight detections logged by the time the sun was fully up. A Tufted Titmouse arrived just six minutes after sunrise, opening the feeder traffic that has since totaled eighty-three visits, far above the recent average of nineteen. The morning built steadily with Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees dominating the feeders, while a Ruby-throated Hummingbird made a brief appearance among the tube feeders.

By mid-morning, Red-bellied Woodpeckers and Eastern Towhees added texture to the constant Wren chorus. A first confident visual record of an American Goldfinch provided a bright flash of color against the usual brown and gray regulars. The feeder activity remained robust through the 9:00 hour, keeping the station lively well past the usual mid-morning lull.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The afternoon quiet gave way to a distinct evening surge, with American Crows and Blue Jays returning in force at 17:00, producing seventeen Crow detections and thirteen Blue Jay calls. A single Northern Mockingbird provided the day’s final visual sighting at 19:31, pushing the total to one hundred and ten feeder visits, vastly exceeding the recent daily average of seven.

Carolina Wrens maintained their persistent presence through dusk, logging nine additional detections in the 19:00 hour to keep their total near seventy-six.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The feeder traffic has slowed considerably since the morning rush, with the last confirmed visual sighting belonging to a Northern Mockingbird at 10:07. This is far quieter than the recent-day average of one and a half visits by this time, though the total of one hundred and two visits remains high. The air is warm at twenty-nine point eight Celsius with light wind and no rain.

Carolina Wrens continue to dominate the auditory landscape, with their calls detected consistently through the midday hours. American Crows provided a loud backdrop in the late morning, but their presence has faded by the afternoon. Tufted Titmice remain the most frequent visual visitors, holding the feeder through the earlier part of the day.

The station’s first confident visual records for a Mourning Dove and a White-breasted Nuthatch were noted earlier, the latter foraging on a metal pole. An adult Blue Jay was also seen foraging on the ground in a grassy area. These new additions to the visual log bring the species count to fourteen, significantly exceeding the recent average of five.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The Tufted Titmouse was already on the wire five minutes before the sun cleared the horizon at 07:06. Carolina Wrens and American Crows provided a steady backdrop of calls in the pre-dawn hours, while the feeder itself remained largely dormant until the Chickadees began their first visits at 07:16.

The morning shifted sharply after 08:00, when the auditory logs filled with nineteen Crows and eleven Blue Jays. This sudden influx brought the total species count to twelve, far exceeding the recent average of four, and pushed the visual visits to a robust seventy-six.

New faces appeared in the mid-morning, including the station’s first confirmed records of a Mourning Dove and a White-breasted Nuthatch. The latter was observed foraging on a nearby metal pole, while an adult Blue Jay perched low in the grass, adding a rare visual texture to the otherwise busy feeder traffic.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The evening brought a marked shift in activity, with twelve of the day's twenty-two visits occurring after 6:30 PM. This final hour was the busiest of the day, dominated by a Northern Mockingbird that appeared three times and a Blue Jay that registered two probable visits alongside a confident Carolina Chickadee. The station’s total of twenty-two visits stands in stark contrast to recent days, which averaged zero visual records up to this hour.

While earlier editions noted the vocal dominance of the Carolina Wren and American Crow, the late evening saw the Blue Jay and Red-bellied Woodpecker emerge as the primary audibly active species, with twelve detections each in the final hour. The Northern Mockingbird, previously absent from the visual log, provided the last clear sighting of the day, perched on a wire at 19:27 just before sunset. This late surge closes out a day that significantly outpaced the recent average of forty-two detections.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The Ruby-throated Hummingbird provided the station’s first visual record of the day, hovering near the feeder at 11:44. This was followed by a Tufted Titmouse at 12:13, which perched on the wire facing right, and a Carolina Wren that visited the feeder at 15:21. These three birds constitute the only confident visual sightings logged so far.

Today’s count of ninety-nine detections is significantly higher than the recent average of twenty-six for this time of day. The Carolina Wren remains the most frequent vocalizer with fifty-seven calls, while the American Crow contributed thirty-seven detections. The Eastern Towhee added twenty-six calls to the afternoon tally.

The weather remains calm with a high of 28.7 C and light winds. A Red-shouldered Hawk passed through at midday, adding five detections to the afternoon record.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The Eastern Screech-Owl held the dark from midnight until dawn, registering eight detections across the pre-sunrise hours. As the light broke at 07:10, the American Crow took over, producing a sudden burst of thirty-three calls in the first hour. A single Red-shouldered Hawk passed through the same window, adding a brief, high-frequency note to the crow’s racket.

By mid-morning, the station has recorded 108 detections and seven species, far outpacing the recent average of ten. The Carolina Wren dominates the count with forty-nine calls, becoming the clear vocal leader. This activity level is a stark contrast to yesterday, which closed with seventy-nine total detections and only five species identified.

No visual sightings have been logged today. The Eastern Towhee contributed twelve detections, peaking in the late morning, while the Blue Jay added two brief notes to the mix.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The evening brought a final surge of sound that doubled the day’s total to seventy-nine detections, far exceeding the recent average of five. This late burst was driven by seven Eastern Towhees and four Red-bellied Woodpeckers, marking the first time since the morning that the woodpecker’s knocks returned with such volume. The Carolina Wren added three more calls to the mix, maintaining its steady presence across the day's final hours.

The American Crow, which dominated the start of the day, reappeared with six detections in the 17:00 hour, though it did not feature in the final evening rush. This late-afternoon activity stands in sharp contrast to yesterday, when all recorded sound arrived in a single cluster just before sunset. The station’s log remains strictly auditory, with no visual contacts or feeder visits recorded despite the increased vocal traffic.

As the light fades after the 19:00 hour, the Red-shouldered Hawk’s earlier presence has quieted, leaving the wrens and towhees to close out the day. The day ended with a sustained volume of sound rather than the singular, brief cluster observed in the previous entry. The station’s record reflects a full day of activity, defined entirely by the birds' voices in the absence of any physical interaction with the feeder.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The midday hours brought a steady rhythm of sound, with the Carolina Wren and Red-bellied Woodpecker providing the majority of the day’s fifty-two total detections. Unlike the single burst recorded in the morning, activity spread evenly across the hours, including a notable presence of Red-shouldered Hawks in the late morning and early afternoon. The weather remains calm and dry, with no precipitation and light winds, while the feeder itself has seen zero physical visits.

As the afternoon progresses, the auditory count has outpaced recent days, where previous records show no data or minimal activity. The Red-bellied Woodpecker continues to register frequently, appearing in four separate hourly blocks throughout the day. This sustained vocal presence contrasts with the lack of visual confirmation, keeping the station’s record strictly limited to sound.

The log concludes with a final check of the species list, confirming that no new birds have been added to the station’s known roster today. The American Crow’s dominance from the morning has faded, replaced by a more balanced mix of wrens, woodpeckers, and jays. With the light still strong and the feeder untouched, the station maintains its quiet, invisible presence until evening.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The morning began with a distinct shift in profile compared to yesterday, as all twenty detections arrived in a single block during the 09:00 hour. This early concentration marks a departure from the late-afternoon clustering observed previously, with American Crows dominating the auditory landscape with ten calls.

The rest of the station’s activity followed the crows, including five Eastern Towhees and two Blue Jays. Red-bellied Woodpeckers added two distinct knocks to the mix, while a single Carolina Wren provided the day's only instance of that species.

With no visual contacts recorded and the feeder remaining untouched, the station’s log rests entirely on this early vocal burst. This marks the first time the station has seen any activity in the morning, breaking the recent pattern of empty ledgers.

posts.heading: September 7, 2026
posts.text:
The day closed with no visual contacts at the feeder, leaving the log to rest entirely on sound. Only two species were detected throughout the period, with the total count remaining quiet at five instances. Since there is no prior data from the recent week, it is difficult to gauge whether this level of activity is typical or exceptional for the station.

All detections arrived in a single cluster during the 19:00 hour, just before sunset. The Carolina Wren accounted for three of the hearing, while the Eastern Towhee provided the remaining two. This late-afternoon concentration meant the earlier hours passed without any recorded activity.

With the light fading and the birds gone, the station ends its first logged day on a hushed note. The lack of feeder visits suggests the birds were moving through the area rather than staying to feed. The log is now closed, awaiting the next day's observations.
